lead: Yesterday was the feast of St Mark, and today's Gospel comes from his book: the parable of the sower, which begins and ends with a call to listen. The Epistle tells us where God's word is now heard most fully. We have not come to the terrors of Sinai but to Mount Zion, the heavenly Jerusalem, and to Jesus, the mediator of a new covenant. The key words are come and listen.

r.h: You have come to Mount Zion
set: Hebrews is a long sermon in written form, addressed to Christians who were growing tired and tempted to fall back. Its author is unknown; the early Church already debated whether Paul wrote it. Chapter 12 urges the readers to run the race with their eyes on Jesus (12:1–2). Today's verses set two mountains side by side, Sinai, where the Law was given (Exodus 19–20; Deuteronomy 4–5), and Zion, the city of God.
str: vv. 18–21: what you have not come to: fire, darkness, trumpet, a voice no one could bear.
vv. 22–24: what you have come to: the city of the living God, angels, the firstborn, God, the righteous, Jesus and his blood.
kw: The verb is in a tense that speaks of arrival with lasting effect: you have come and you are here. It is also the word Hebrews uses for drawing near to God in worship (4:16; 10:22).
Ekklēsia is the word for the Church. The firstborn belonged to God in Israel (Exodus 13:2). Here all the faithful, “enrolled in heaven”, share that title in Christ, “the firstborn” (1:6).
The one who stands between two parties and binds them. Moses was mediator at Sinai; Jesus is mediator of the new covenant, and his own blood seals it (9:15).
vv: Indeed, so terrifying was the sight that Moses said, “I tremble with fear.”
These words are not found in the Sinai story of Exodus. They echo Deuteronomy 9:19, where Moses fears God's anger after the golden calf. Even the great mediator of the old covenant trembled.
But you have come to Mount Zion and to the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem, and to innumerable angels in festal gathering,
The Christian is not waiting outside. In worship he is already joined to the festival of heaven, though still on the way.
and to Jesus, the mediator of a new covenant, and to the sprinkled blood that speaks a better word than the blood of Abel.
Abel's blood cried out from the ground for justice (Genesis 4:10). The blood of Jesus speaks of mercy and forgiveness.
ch: The Church reads this passage as a description of her worship. The Second Vatican Council says that in the earthly liturgy we share in a foretaste of the heavenly liturgy celebrated in the holy city of Jerusalem, toward which we journey as pilgrims (Sacrosanctum Concilium 8; CCC 1090). The contrast is not between a cruel God and a kind one. The same God spoke at Sinai and speaks in his Son. What is new is that, through Jesus, the distance has been crossed.

r.h: A sower went out to sow
set: Mark gathers several parables in chapter 4. Jesus has already met growing opposition (3:6, 22) and has chosen the Twelve (3:13–19). Now he teaches from a boat, with the crowd on the shore. The explanation of the parable comes later, given to the disciples (4:13–20); today we hear the story as the crowd heard it.
str: vv. 1–2: the setting: the boat, the crowd, teaching in parables.
vv. 3–8: the sower and four kinds of ground.
kw: Behind it is the Hebrew māshāl, which covers proverbs, riddles and stories. A parable draws the hearer in and leaves him to find the meaning, so it reveals to some and hides from others (4:11–12).
The parable opens with this command and closes with “Let anyone with ears to hear listen!” Israel's great prayer begins the same way: “Hear, O Israel” (Deuteronomy 6:4).
vv: Listen! A sower went out to sow.
The sower scatters seed everywhere, even on the path and among stones. God does not first measure the soil before he speaks.
Other seed fell on rocky ground, where it did not have much soil, and it sprang up quickly, since it had no depth of soil.
Quick growth is not the same as deep growth. Jesus later explains that these are people who receive the word with joy but fall away when trouble comes (4:16–17).
Other seed fell into good soil and brought forth grain, growing up and increasing and yielding thirty and sixty and a hundredfold.
After three losses, a harvest beyond all expectation. Even Isaac's blessed harvest is called a hundredfold (Genesis 26:12). The parable ends in hope.
ch: The Church hears the parable as a call to examine the soil of the heart. The Catechism uses it to speak of the Kingdom: the word is like seed sown in a field, and those who hear it with faith have received the Kingdom itself (CCC 543). The Second Vatican Council quotes Jesus' saying that the word of the Lord is like a seed sown in a field (Lumen Gentium 5). For a family, the parable asks practical questions: what birds, rocks and thorns stop the word from growing in our home?

qa: Is the parable saying that some people are simply bad soil and cannot change?

No. A parable is a call, not a verdict. Jesus speaks so that the hearers will become good soil. The paths can be broken up, the stones removed and the thorns pulled out, and the grace of God is the farmer who does it with our consent.
study: Which of the four kinds of ground best describes how I heard last Sunday's word?
Hebrews says we have already come to the heavenly Jerusalem. How would I take part in the Holy Qurbono differently if I believed that?
